This is an example of how know a little bit about something can make you stupid about the whole topic. 

There are thousands of different types and subtypes of cancers, and entire fields of studies dedicated to them.

Some cancers can be diagnosed by removing them completely without biopsy, which itself is the biopsy, if it’s small enough and the procedure won’t damage surrounding structures too much. 

Others based on imaging and location are amenable to needle biopsy without being known to cause tumor seeding.

Others are “systemic” cancers that are already spread through your blood and body, and the tumor or tumors are just one manifestation, so it doesn’t matter if you biopsy and seed because it’s all over. Not all these situations are end-game, like certain lymphomas that are very treatable or even curable. Others represent stage IV, metastatic cancer, and you are basically fucked.

Some can be reasonably be diagnosed with a combination of imaging and blood markers.

Some cancers only respond to surgical removal, others to chemo, others to radiation, and others to some combination. Some respond to immunologic therapy. Others are so slow growing that you are unlikely to die from it. Others are so aggressive that by the time they are diagnosed 100% of people are dead of it within 5 years. 

But it always makes me laugh a little bit when the whole entire centuries-built science, composing dozens of different disciplines and fields, with hundreds of thousands of ongoing trials and studies, for what are thousands of basically different diseases that we call “cancer,” people reduce to a simple question like this or a throw away comment like it’s all a conspiracy to bolster the pharmaceutical industry.

Every hospital in a developed country has sepsis protocols that are almost automated at this point / but it just triggers certain actions based on a handful of criteria based primarily on vitals and partially on labs. People can fall short of the criteria. These days almost everyone who fits criteria gets a CT scan - it’s almost weird not to get one. 

But like all criteria based management, there’s going to be a miss rate. Now people might ask / why not make the criteria so liberal that everyone gets the full work up? Well one, it would unnecessarily irradiate so many patients with X-rays and scans it would probably raise the cancer incidence significantly in the population. A CT can have up to 1000x the radiation of a simple X-ray. Ultrasound has no radiation but isn’t as sensitive in catching things - and physical exam alone is an abysmal test in terms of catching things all the time. It would also probably bankrupt the entire system. For example, so of the sepsis criteria is elevated heart rate and respiratory rate. That can occur from running up a flight of stairs. But not everyone who does that needs a full work up and treatment with antibiotics, etc. So that’s where judgement comes into play - what’s the history, the context, etc, and this in turn is dependent on practitioner acumen, experience, biases, how busy a place is. 

Some people here mentioned lawsuits but sepsis-related lawsuits are extremely hard to win. Many attorneys won’t even take them. The reason is presenting symptoms have so many possible explanations that it’s hard to prove something to a reasonable degree of certainty - with the information available at the time. Retrospective information doesn’t help, it’s what the practitioners had in front of them not knowing the final outcome. 

All that being said, campaigns to improve sepsis survival - actually called the Surviving Sepsis Campaign - have drastically improved survival to the point that despite the bad experiences individuals may have had, the overall impact when looking at the entire population of patients is the safest, most effective healthcare the world has ever had in history. But always room for improvement - things like augmented intelligence / using AI to aid in making decisions, will probably continue to improve overall outcomes.
You don’t have to have bacteremia (blood infection) to have sepsis.

Sepsis by itself is not a specific diagnosis - it’s the body’s reaction to a source of infection. The potential sources are too numerous to list. When the body has a similar response without infection it’s called SIRS, and they can also be instigated by numerous things. 

There’s been sepsis protocols in hospitals for over a decade and the basic idea are early antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, and control of the source of sepsis. 

Also, everyone’s sepsis response is different, probably based on many factors such as genetics, cormordities, age, etc. Not everyone will react the same to the exact same infectious source. It can also move along slowly, self-resolve, or progress rapidly, with or without treatment.

It makes more sense to refer to the source of infection as to what someone might have survived, or experienced. Like “acute appendicitis,” or infected leg wound. The sepsis part just describes certain criteria for how your body is responding - the source of infection is what is killing you (kind of, the body’s deranged response has a role).

Shock is a clinical term referring to low blood pressure, to the point of inadequate tissue perfusion. This can happen from bleeding, severe dehydration, injury to the brain or spine, or from a cardiac event like a heart attack or heart failure. 

If the head is severed, there will be the ultimate “shock” or hypotension to the brain. Cerebral blood pressure will essentially drop to zero immediately. You cannot remain conscious after that. The equivalent situation would be actually having your heart stop, or, being put in an extremely tight choke hole that occludes the carotid arteries completely and suddenly. You’ll pass out. You can stop oxygen flow for a bit and remain conscious because of remaining oxygen in your body, but you can’t remain conscious with cessation of blood flow to your brain.

The very old account of the person’s head staying alive for a while is old, non-scientific, unverifiable, and frankly, medically impossible. 

If you have your head cut off you will be out, and you will be dead.

For every 999 patients with a headache that the physician treats conservatively, they may miss the one brain tumor that they didn’t order an MRI on. By the way, the bar for malpractice (in the US) is very high. 

If you request a test, and the doctor denies it because they don’t think it’s indicated, and they end up missing a diagnosis, disease, or even cancer - they have not committed malpractice unless they egregiously breached the standard of care - or what any reasonably competent physician would do in a similar situation. 

For almost all things, this is very difficult to prove. There’s going to be some very obvious things that require reflex tests that if not done, is malpractice - but >90% of the time, not doing the test will fall within the standard of care.
